claims.text: The component material is prone to hot cracking under fusion-welding conditions.
Defects in the component preclude effective traditional fusion-welding repair.
Laser cladding can be used to deposit a functional repair coating on a substrate surface.
A FeCrNiTiZr high-entropy-alloy coating is a suitable repair material with high hardness and good elevated-temperature wear resistance.
Controlled laser cladding minimizes heat input and dilution relative to conventional fusion welding.
Minimizing heat input and dilution avoids low-melting secondary phases that promote hot cracking.
Laser cladding will produce a refined, single-phase repair layer with minimal segregation.
The laser-clad repair layer will be metallurgically bonded to the substrate.
The repair layer will lack the low-melting-point phases responsible for hot cracking.
Rapid solidification during laser cladding reduces local thermal input and suppresses detrimental microstructural transformations.
Laser cladding avoids the formation of wide freezing ranges and low-melting secondary phases.
The refined repair-layer microstructure minimizes residual stresses.
Reduced residual stress and suppression of detrimental phases prevent hot cracking and restore mechanical integrity.
The laser-clad repair will be crack-free or exhibit significantly less hot cracking than a conventional fusion-weld repair.
The laser-clad repair will provide better elevated-temperature wear resistance than conventional fusion-weld repair.
The laser-clad repair will provide better surface fatigue resistance than conventional fusion-weld repair.
The repair is intended to operate under elevated temperatures, wear, fatigue loading, and mechanical stress.
Repair performance will depend on the specific HEA composition and laser-cladding process parameters.
